h: The Room Dr Johnson Couldn't Stop Praising
p: Newhailes started life in the late seventeenth century, when the architect James Smith built it as his own home. The Dalrymples bought it in the early 1700s and stayed for generations, and they were a bookish bunch. Their library was so impressive that Dr Samuel Johnson is said to have called it the most learned room in Europe. Not bad for a house on the edge of Musselburgh.

What makes Newhailes feel different from many grand houses is how it has been cared for. Rather than being polished up to look brand new, it has been conserved largely as it was found, with faded paint, worn fabrics and the patina of centuries left in place. It gives the rooms a real, lived-in feel, almost as if the family have just popped out. Keep that in mind on the tour; the imperfections are part of the story, not a sign of neglect.

Who's it for? History lovers and anyone who enjoys a quieter, more thoughtful country house will be in their element, while young families can lean heavily on the woods and play park. Give yourselves at least half a day if you want both the house and the grounds without a rush. Afterwards, Musselburgh itself is worth a mooch. It's known as the Honest Toun, the River Esk runs right through the middle, and Luca's ice cream has been a local treat for over a century. Edinburgh is only a short hop by train or bus if you fancy rounding off the day in the capital.
